true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Global group canManage() grants manage rights for VIEW permission

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when the caller has either VIEW or MANAGE on the Groups resource type. This method is used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup through requireManage(), so a permission that only grants view on all groups allows creating or moving top-level groups. Global manage should require MANAGE only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts VIEW as well as MANAGE, which gives view-only users manage access. The fix both describe is to require MANAGE only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds groupResource.getId() to the returned set. Callers such as UsersResource.searchForUser and UsersResource.getUsersCount expect group IDs, but authorization resource IDs are internal IDs. The loop also processes the type resource named Groups. As a result, user search and count can filter on wrong IDs and return incorrect or empty results when group member-view permissions are used. The code should skip the type resource and add the resource name, which is the group ID.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds the resource ID (groupResource.getId()) instead of the group ID (the resource name). Both also note that callers filtering and counting users then get wrong IDs, and both suggest using resource names instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Individual authorization resources are created without a resource type

AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates individual resources for users, clients, and groups with a name and scopes but never calls resource.setType(resourceType). GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission relies on resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to enumerate group resources, so individually created group resources will not be found. This breaks enumeration of group-scoped permissions for user search and counts.

V2 group permissions throw UnsupportedOperationException from existing lifecycle/API paths

GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but existing code still calls it. AdminPermissions.registerListener calls management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) on GroupRemovedEvent, and GroupResource.setManagementPermissionsEnabled calls it through the groups management/permissions endpoint. When V2 is active this can cause group deletion events to fail or the REST endpoint to return 500, and no cleanup of group authorization resources is performed.

Group permission evaluation does not filter granted permissions by resource ID

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission evaluates permissions for a group resource but does not filter returned Permission objects by resource ID. UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission performs this filter, which is necessary when evaluation can include permissions attached to the resource type or other resources. Without the filter, all-groups permissions may be treated as granted during group-specific checks even when a specific group resource exists, potentially bypassing intended restrictions or negative permissions.

getScope can throw NullPointerException for unknown resource type

AdminPermissionsSchema.getScope calls SCHEMA.getResourceTypes().get(resourceType).getScopes() without checking whether resourceType is null or whether the map lookup returns null. A null or unknown resource type will cause a NullPointerException instead of a validation error, turning invalid input into a 500 response.

getOrCreateResource throws IllegalStateException for unknown entity IDs

AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource throws IllegalStateException when resolveGroup, resolveUser, or resolveClient returns null. A REST caller creating a scope permission with a non-existent group, user, or client ID can trigger a 500 response instead of a 400/404 validation error.

getResourceName does not resolve group resource names

AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName only resolves user resources. For group resources it returns resource.getDisplayName(), but individual group resources are created with the group ID as the name and no display name. Admin UI or policy representations will therefore show an empty value or internal ID instead of the group name.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length ASN.1 integer causes NegativeArraySizeException

readLength can return -1 for indefinite-length encoding, but readInteger passes that value directly to read(int), which allocates new byte[length]. A malformed DER signature using indefinite length will therefore cause NegativeArraySizeException instead of an IOException. The decoder should reject indefinite-length encodings in this DER-oriented use case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments trace the problem to the -1 length that readLength returns for indefinite-length encoding and say it is mishandled downstream. They point at different symptoms: the golden comment flags the arithmetic 'length - bytes.length', while the candidate flags a NegativeArraySizeException in readInteger. The root cause is the same unhandled -1 length, so they likely refer to the same underlying bug, though the specific location differs somewhat.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New non-default order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public interface, and this PR adds int order() as an abstract method. Any existing implementation compiled against the previous interface will fail to compile against the new API and can fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when provider selection calls order(). Adding a default order() implementation would preserve compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that adding an abstract order() method to the CryptoProvider interface breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations. The candidate goes further and suggests a default implementation as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Provider selection is undefined when multiple providers have the same order

detectProvider sorts discovered CryptoProvider instances only by order() and then picks the first one. Existing full providers such as DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200. If two providers with the same order are present, the selected provider depends on ServiceLoader iteration order, while the others are only logged at debug level. A misconfigured classpath can therefore silently select the wrong crypto provider.

Ignored crypto providers are still instantiated and may mutate global security state

detectProvider loads and instantiates every discovered CryptoProvider before choosing one. Some providers perform global JCA registration or security-property changes in their constructors, for example FIPS1402Provider. Because this PR allows multiple providers to be present and only selects the highest-order one, an ignored provider can still register security providers or alter JVM-wide security state even though it is not the selected CryptoProvider.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate the input signature length

concatenatedRSToASN1DER assumes the supplied signature array has exactly signLength bytes. If it is shorter, System.arraycopy throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; if it is longer, extra bytes are silently ignored. Malformed signature input should be validated and rejected with IOException instead.

ECDSA conversion silently truncates oversized integer values

In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes copies only the last qLength bytes when BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than expected. For a malformed DER signature whose R or S value is larger than the expected coordinate size, high-order bytes are silently discarded instead of rejecting the signature. This can hide malformed input and produce an incorrect concatenated RS signature.

ECDSA test does not use curve-appropriate keys or verify conversion correctness

The test generates one default EC key pair and uses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. For ES384 and ES512 this likely exercises smaller coordinates than the real target curves, mostly testing padding rather than full-size values. It also only asserts that concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS is stable, not that the re-encoded DER matches the original signature or that the converted signature verifies, so incorrect conversion logic could still pass.

false_positives.candidate:
SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool

The strategy is constructed with the FixedQueuePool that ResultsStrategyFactory creates once and reuses. close() ultimately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), permanently stopping the worker threads and queues. Arroyo can create a new processing strategy after rebalances using the same factory, so any later strategy would be backed by a dead pool and would not process messages. Strategy close should only stop its own commit thread, or the factory must create/reset a pool per strategy.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() calls put() without blocking or rejecting. If a group assigned to a queue is slow, the consumer continues polling and enqueueing work indefinitely. This can grow memory and offset-tracking state without bound and potentially OOM the consumer, despite the docstring claiming natural backpressure.

Failed work items are marked completed and can be committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run catches Exception from the result processor and then unconditionally marks the offset complete in finally. ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows handle_result exceptions. A message that fails processing is therefore treated as done and can be committed by the background commit loop, permanently skipping it. This contradicts the stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing; failures need retry, DLQ, or explicit drop handling.

Submission errors silently drop messages and mark offsets complete

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions from decoding, grouping, or enqueueing and, when the message has broker metadata, adds the offset and immediately completes it. A malformed payload or a bug in grouping_fn can therefore cause the message to be skipped while its offset becomes committable. There is no DLQ, retry, or failure metric to make this data loss visible.

close() stops the commit loop before draining the queue pool

close() sets the shutdown event, joins the commit thread, and only then shuts down the FixedQueuePool. If queue_pool.shutdown() processes any remaining queued items, those items complete after the last commit opportunity, so their offsets will not be committed and they will be reprocessed after restart. The shutdown order should allow draining and then perform a final commit, or commit while draining.

OffsetTracker state persists across partition assignments

OffsetTracker is owned by the long-lived FixedQueuePool and is never reset or pruned when partitions are revoked or reassigned. Outstanding offsets from a revoked partition can remain forever. If the same partition is later reassigned with different offsets, a stale outstanding offset can create an artificial gap that blocks get_committable_offsets() from committing newer offsets, and old partition state leaks.

Committable-offset calculation scans potentially huge offset ranges

get_committable_offsets() iterates over every integer offset from the first possible uncommitted offset through max(all_offsets). If one old offset remains outstanding because of a slow worker, shutdown loss, or stale tracker state, this scan is repeated every commit cycle and can become very expensive for large offset ranges, while also hiding the fact that one offset is stuck.

max_workers is not validated for positive values

In thread-queue-parallel mode the pool is created with num_queues=max_workers or 20. Passing --max-workers 0 silently becomes 20, and passing a negative value creates a pool with no queues, leading to IndexError or modulo issues when submitting work. The CLI option or factory should validate that max_workers is greater than zero.

Error-handling test asserts behavior the implementation does not guarantee

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling makes the result processor raise for one message and asserts that no offset is committed. However the worker catches the exception and marks the offset complete, so the background commit loop can commit it if it runs before the test shuts everything down. The test currently depends on shutting down before the commit timer fires, making it flaky and validating the wrong contract.

WorkItem retains the full Kafka message unnecessarily

WorkItem stores the original Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload], but workers only use partition, offset, and result. Keeping the full Kafka payload in queues increases memory usage, which is especially problematic because the queues are unbounded. The message field can be removed or replaced with only the needed metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Span buffer keys are changed from Redis sets to sorted sets without migration

The previous implementation stored span payloads in Redis sets using sadd, scard, sunionstore, and sscan. This change makes the Lua script and Python buffer operate on the same span-buf:s:* keys as sorted sets using zcard, zunionstore, zpopmin, zadd, and zscan. During deployment, in-flight keys created by the old code will still be sets, so new operations will fail with WRONGTYPE and span ingestion or flushing can break. A key namespace change, migration, or drain is needed.

ZUNIONSTORE uses the default SUM aggregation and can corrupt span scores

The sorted-set members are span payloads and their scores are end_timestamp_precise. ZUNIONSTORE is called without AGGREGATE MIN or MAX, so if a member exists in both source sets, for example due to duplicate messages or a span being present in both an old and merged buffer, Redis adds the two scores together. The resulting timestamp score is wrong, which can cause incorrect eviction ordering and make some spans never eligible for zpopmin.

When a merged span buffer has more than 1000 members, the script pops and discards the lowest-scored members. There is no metric, log, or tombstone indicating that spans were dropped, and the eviction can remove spans needed to assemble a complete segment, including potentially important root or parent spans. Flushed segments can therefore be incomplete without any observable signal. The limit is also hardcoded in Lua and ignores the Python max_segment_spans configuration.

The script follows at most 1000 redirect hops to find the canonical span buffer. If a redirect chain is longer than that, it stops early and stores the new span against an intermediate set instead of the final merged set. This can split a single trace segment into multiple buffers and produce incomplete or duplicated flushed segments. The previous limit was 10000, so this increases the correctness risk for deep or pathological traces.

The datetime incompatibility and negative-offset behavior introduced by this paginator are therefore unverified, and regressions in this privileged pagination path would not be caught.

The PR introduces sorted-set storage, score-based eviction at 1000 spans, and a reduced redirect-depth limit, but the updated tests only add end_timestamp_precise to small fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans, verifies which spans are evicted, checks behavior when duplicate members are merged, or exercises redirect chains near the new limit.

This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous and can collide across resources

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with underscores. Resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different (name, parent) tuples can produce the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="" and name="a" with parent="b" both serialize to the suffix "_a_b_". Because a denial-cache hit short-circuits the authorization check, a denial cached for one resource/folder combination can be incorrectly applied to another, causing authorized requests to be denied for the cache TTL. Use an unambiguous escaping, separator scheme, or hash of the fields.

Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity denials

Check builds the denial-cache key from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder only; the identity type is not included. Supported subjects include anonymous:0 and render:0, both of which parse to the identifier "0". A denied check for anonymous will therefore write a denial entry that a subsequent renderer check with the same action/resource/folder will hit, causing the renderer to be denied even though renderer permissions are hard-coded to allow dashboard/folder/datasource reads. The reverse is also possible. The denial key should include the identity type.

Cached denial can continue to deny after permissions are granted

Check returns false immediately when a denial-cache entry exists, and denial entries are written after any failed full check with a 30-second TTL. If access is granted immediately after a denial, for example when permissions are added around dashboard/folder creation, subsequent checks for that exact resource will keep hitting the denial cache and will be denied until the TTL expires. This can still block access to newly created resources, which is the issue this PR is intended to fix. Consider invalidating negative entries on permission changes, avoiding negative caching in this path, or using a much shorter TTL.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

If an existing Integration lacks metadata.sender, sender is not a dict, login is absent, or metadata is None (legacy rows, webhook payloads without sender, or integrations created before this change), this raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of the intended error page. false_positives.candidate:
Ownership check is skipped when the Integration row does not exist

The authenticated GitHub user is only checked when an active Integration row already exists. When Integration.DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() and build_integration will create the integration from the supplied installation_id without proving that the OAuth-authenticated user controls that installation. If a Sentry Integration record is absent because the webhook was delayed/failed or the data is legacy, a user who supplies a known installation_id could bind someone else's GitHub App installation to their organization. The flow should fail closed or verify ownership before advancing.

Token exchange and user fetch can 500 instead of showing the failure page

OAuthLoginView exchanges the OAuth code and fetches user info, but only parsing of the token response is wrapped in try/except. safe_urlopen and get_user_info can raise on network failures, timeouts, or non-successful GitHub responses. In those cases the request will return a 500 rather than the intended github-integration-failed error response. These calls should be guarded and return error() on failure.

OAuthLoginView binds installation_id from the query string on every dispatch, including OAuth callback requests, and does so before validating the state parameter. GitHub does not include installation_id in the OAuth redirect, so a crafted callback can alter the pipeline's stored installation_id, or mutate pipeline state even when state validation fails. The redirect to GitHub's authorize endpoint is built by interpolating client_id, state, and redirect_uri directly into a query string. redirect_uri contains characters such as ':' and '/' and should be percent-encoded per OAuth/form-urlencoded requirements. Use urllib.parse.urlencode to construct the URL; otherwise the request may be rejected by stricter OAuth servers/proxies, and future values with special characters could break the redirect.

If a request has setup_action=install and no pipeline but lacks installation_id, the code calls reverse('integration-installation', args=[provider_id, None]). Depending on the URL route converter this can generate an invalid URL or raise. Validate that installation_id is present before reversing, and otherwise redirect to a safe fallback.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. More importantly, a caller that observed a nil cache before another goroutine populated it can still run the load path and, if that load fails, the unconditional assignment at line 69 can overwrite a valid cached value with nil. Re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock for non-dev mode, and/or avoid replacing a valid cache when the reload fails.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.reasoning: Both flag swapped duration-recording functions in DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection error path. The golden comment's wording is ambiguous about which direction the mixup goes, but both describe the same legacy/storage metric misattribution.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete storage duration metric uses object name as kind label

In Delete, the success path records storage duration with name as the third argument: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Other methods pass options.Kind for that label. This puts the resource name into the kind metric label, producing incorrect metrics and potentially high-cardinality series, breaking dashboards or alerts that aggregate by kind. It should pass options.Kind.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the metrics recording passes name where options.Kind belongs, which is inconsistent with the other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes use the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes

Create derives the background legacy-write context from the incoming request context using context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The same pattern is used in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. When the HTTP handler returns, the request context is canceled, so the child context is also canceled even though the legacy write is intended to continue asynchronously. This can abort legacy writes immediately after the API response is sent, defeating mode 3's dual-write safety behavior and causing divergence between unified storage and legacy storage. Use a detached context such as context.WithoutCancel(ctx), or a dedicated background context that preserves values but not cancellation.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes are unordered and untracked

Each write path launches an independent goroutine to create, update, delete, or delete-collection in legacy storage. There is no ordering, queue, mutex, wait group, or lifecycle tracking. Concurrent operations on the same object may complete in legacy storage in a different order than they were applied to unified storage, for example a delete arriving before a create or an old update arriving after a newer update. This can leave legacy storage inconsistent with unified storage. Destroy may also run while these goroutines are still active. If legacy writes are meant to be a safe fallback, they should be serialized per object or managed by a tracked background worker.

Background legacy-write goroutines do not recover from panics

The asynchronous legacy write paths use bare goroutines without panic recovery. Because legacy writes are secondary and best-effort in mode 3, a panic in legacy storage code or serialization should not crash the whole API server process. Add a deferred recover in these goroutines and log/metric the failure.

Legacy update is performed with the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage

After Storage.Update succeeds, the code asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will re-evaluate UpdatedObject against the legacy store's current object, which may produce a different result than the update that was applied in unified storage, especially for patches, defaults, generated fields, or resourceVersion handling. Mode 3 treats unified storage as the source of truth, so legacy should receive the final object returned by Storage.Update. The previous implementation wrapped the updated object for the legacy call; removing that wrapper creates a real risk of silent divergence between unified storage and legacy storage.

Legacy create uses the original request object instead of the created object

After Storage.Create succeeds, the asynchronous Legacy.Create call is made with the original obj rather than the created object returned by unified storage. If unified storage assigns a name, UID, creation timestamp, defaults, or otherwise changes the object, legacy storage may create a different object identity or fail validation. To mirror unified storage, the legacy create should use the created object's identity and spec, clearing any fields that are invalid on create such as resourceVersion if needed.

Storage Delete errors, including NotFound, prevent legacy cleanup

Delete returns immediately when Storage.Delete fails, so Legacy.Delete is never attempted. The previous implementation treated NotFound specially and still attempted deletion from legacy storage. If an object exists only in legacy storage, or remains there after unified storage no longer has it, this change can leave stale legacy data that may reappear if the dual-writer mode changes. The same issue exists for DeleteCollection, where any storage error skips legacy cleanup. At minimum, NotFound from unified storage should still trigger legacy deletion.

Storage create failures are recorded as legacy duration

When Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This misattributes a unified-storage failure and latency to legacy storage. Operators relying on dual-writer metrics will see false legacy errors and missing storage errors. Use recordStorageDuration for the storage operation.

Storage update failures are recorded as legacy duration

When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This misattributes a unified-storage failure and latency to legacy storage. Use recordStorageDuration for the storage operation so mode 3 metrics correctly distinguish unified storage failures from legacy failures.

Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged

In Create, errors from Legacy.Create are only reflected in a metric. The same applies to the asynchronous legacy operations in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Since mode 3 writes to legacy storage as a safety measure, silent failures make it difficult to diagnose divergence. Log the error with the object kind, name or identifier, and operation before recording the metric.

Mode 3 unit tests do not wait for or verify asynchronous legacy writes

TestMode3_Create calls dw.Create and returns immediately, but the legacy create happens in a goroutine. The tests do not synchronize with that goroutine, do not assert that legacy methods were actually called, and use a shared mock for both legacy and unified storage, so calls to either store are indistinguishable. As a result, the tests can pass even if asynchronous legacy writes are skipped, canceled, reordered, or otherwise broken. Similar gaps exist for Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Add synchronization and explicit assertions that legacy storage receives the expected calls.

Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous legacy writes

The added mode 3 scenarios run doPlaylistTests, which performs create/update/delete operations through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the change. This makes the integration test flaky and also masks eventual-consistency behavior. The test should poll or otherwise wait for legacy convergence, or mode 3 tests should use a synchronous/test-only legacy write path.

Anonymous.Authenticate fails the first request, but a retry with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id header gets a cache hit, TagDevice returns nil, and the request is authenticated even though the device was not stored and the configured limit should block it. The anonymous device identifier is supplied by the client in the X-Grafana-Device-Id header. With device_limit enabled, unauthenticated callers can create arbitrary unique device IDs until the configured number of active devices is reached. Those attacker-created records remain active for the 30-day window, after which new legitimate devices receive ErrDeviceLimitReached and cannot authenticate, causing a denial of service for new anonymous users.

The PR changes anonymous device tagging from an asynchronous goroutine to a synchronous step in Authenticate. When device_limit is enabled, each uncached device performs a COUNT over anon_device and an upsert before the request can proceed. For high-traffic anonymous instances, especially if updated_at is not efficiently indexed, this can add significant latency and database load to anonymous authentication.

GrafanaConfig declares anonymousDeviceLimit as number | undefined, but the Go FrontendSettingsDTO uses a non-pointer int64 without omitempty, so the backend always sends a number, with 0 meaning unlimited. Frontend code that checks for undefined to determine whether a limit is configured will not work; the contract should either use a pointer/omitempty or document 0 as unlimited.

device_limit is read with MustInt64(0) and enforcement only occurs when the value is greater than zero. A negative configuration value is accepted and silently treated as unlimited, which can hide operator mistakes. The setting should be validated as non-negative.

false_positives.candidate:
Import stores unsanitized remote HTML as raw_html posts

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with skip_validations and cook_method raw_html from fetched/RSS content. Post#cook returns raw for this method and the embed view outputs post.cooked with `raw`, so untrusted HTML from the remote page/feed is stored and rendered without sanitization. This can lead to stored XSS, for example via javascript: links or other active content.

Remote import uses open-uri without redirect or timeout restrictions

`import_remote` fetches URLs with `open(url).read`. open-uri follows redirects and has no connect/read timeout by default. Since the URL can be triggered through embed retrieval, a redirect from an allowed host can be used to reach unintended hosts/internal services, and a slow endpoint can hang the job. Use a restricted HTTP client with timeouts and controlled redirects.

Unknown embed URLs trigger a synchronous full feed poll

When feed polling is enabled, each missing embed URL runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline. This downloads and imports the entire feed just to check for one URL. Anonymous embed requests can enqueue many RetrieveTopic jobs, throttled only per URL, causing repeated expensive feed polling and Sidekiq backlog.

content_sha1 is updated even if the post revision fails

In the update path, `embed.update_column(:content_sha1, content_sha1)` is called after `revise!` without checking the result or rescuing save failures. If the revision does not persist, the embed record still records the new hash, so future imports will think the content is up to date and will not retry.

Loading response is cached for one minute

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is called even when the controller renders the loading page. If the loading response is cached, the iframe's 30-second reload can continue to show the cached loading page after the background job has created the topic. The loading state should be non-cacheable or expire much sooner.

Throttle key set and expiry are not atomic

`$redis.setnx` followed by `$redis.expire` is not atomic. If the process dies between the two commands, the key can remain forever without a TTL, permanently blocking retrieval for that embed URL. Use an atomic SET with NX and EX, or an equivalent atomic primitive.

Blank embed_url is accepted and enqueues a failing job

`params.require(:embed_url)` only requires the key to be present; an empty string passes. The controller then enqueues RetrieveTopic with a blank embed_url, and the job raises Discourse::InvalidParameters. Validate presence/non-blank before enqueuing.

Embed URLs are not normalized before lookup/create

TopicEmbed records are matched by exact `embed_url`. Equivalent URLs, such as http vs https, trailing slash differences, or harmless query/fragment variations, will be treated as different embeds and can create duplicate topics for the same article. Canonicalize URLs before lookup and storage.

Only root-relative URLs are absolutized

`absolutize_urls` rewrites only `href`/`src` values that start with `/`. Relative paths without a leading slash and protocol-relative URLs like `//host/...` are left unchanged, so imported posts can contain broken links/images. Resolve all relative URLs against the source URL.

No guard when #discourse-comments is missing

The script calls `comments.appendChild(iframe)` without checking whether `document.getElementById('discourse-comments')` returned null. If the embedding page lacks that element, JavaScript throws and the embed iframe is never inserted.

Assumes discourseUrl ends with a trailing slash

The iframe src is built by concatenating `discourseUrl` with `embed/best...`. If `discourseUrl` does not end with `/`, the resulting URL is invalid, for example `https://forum.example.comembed/best`. Normalize the base URL before concatenating.

create_table uses force: true

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` will drop an existing `topic_embeds` table and its data before creating the new one. Production migrations should not silently drop tables; use `create_table` without `force` and handle pre-existing tables explicitly if needed.

Existing migration changed to force table recreation

This edits an existing migration and adds `force: true` to `create_table :top_topics`. If the migration is rerun or run after the table already exists, it will drop and recreate the table, causing data loss. Migrations should generally be immutable and not use force in this way.

Loading page reloads forever if retrieval never succeeds

The loading template reloads the page every 30 seconds indefinitely. If the embed cannot be retrieved due to an invalid URL, host mismatch, or remote errors, this creates an endless request loop on the embedding page. Add a failure state or backoff.

Template assumes post.user is present

The embed view calls `post.user.small_avatar_url` and `post.user.username` without nil checks. If a displayed post has a deleted or missing user, the template raises NoMethodError and the embed fails to render. Use a fallback user/display for nil users.

Feed fetch has no timeout/error handling

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` is called without timeouts or rescue. A slow or unresponsive feed can hang the scheduled Sidekiq job and delay other scheduled work. Use an HTTP client with connect/read timeouts and handle fetch errors.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Duplicate `downsize` definition overwrites the four-argument method

Ruby does not overload methods by arity. The second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` replaces the preceding four-argument `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`. The four-argument version is dead code, and any existing caller using width/height will have `height` interpreted as `opts`, likely causing errors or malformed ImageMagick dimensions. If both signatures are needed, use distinct method names or a single method that normalizes arguments.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The second downsize definition, which takes a dimensions string, overrides the first one that takes separate width and height. This leaves the original unreachable and breaks existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Client-side upload size limit hardcoded to 10 MB

The validation now uses a fixed `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. This ignores the configured maximum for both images and attachments: attachments larger than the site limit can be selected/uploaded, and images may be blocked even if the configured image limit is larger than 10 MB. It also makes client-side enforcement inconsistent with the server-side behavior introduced in this PR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the hardcoded 10*1024 KB limit, which ignores the per-type site setting and lets client-side validation diverge from the server. The candidate does not mention the 413 handler, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message uses hardcoded 10 MB limit

On HTTP 413 the code reports `max_size_kb: 10 * 1024` instead of the relevant site setting. Users can be told the limit is 10 MB even when the configured maximum image or attachment size is different, so the error message no longer reflects the actual upload policy.

URL uploads are downloaded with a fixed 10 MB limit

`FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` replaces the previous `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` limit and is used before knowing whether the URL is an image. API URL uploads can now fetch up to 10 MB even when the configured maximum is lower, and non-image/attachment URL uploads are not subject to the attachment limit. This can bypass site limits and waste bandwidth or memory.

Downsizing overwrites the input tempfile in place

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the same path as input and output. ImageMagick/gifsicle are not guaranteed to safely overwrite the file they are reading, and in-place rewriting can truncate or corrupt the original upload if the tool opens the output for writing before fully reading the input or if the operation fails. A temporary output file should be created and atomically replace the original only on success.

Failed or ineffective downsizing is ignored

The loop does not check the boolean returned by `OptimizedImage.downsize` and does not abort if the file is still larger than `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` after five attempts. If conversion fails, the code will retry pointlessly and then continue to `Upload.create_for` with an unchanged or corrupted file, possibly storing an invalid or oversized upload or returning a confusing error.

Tempfile path lacks original extension, breaking animation/format detection

The automatic downsize passes `tempfile.path` to `OptimizedImage.optimize`, which only uses the animated code path when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. Rack/Tempfile paths for uploads usually do not carry the original filename extension, so GIFs will not be detected as animated and will be processed by ImageMagick with `[0]`, stripping animation even when `allow_animation` is enabled. The missing extension can also make ImageMagick choose the wrong output format. Use a temp file with the original extension or pass the desired format explicitly.

SVG/vector images are downsized like raster images

The condition treats any filename matching `FileHelper.is_image?` as resizable, which includes SVG in Discourse. Unlike `OptimizedImage.create_for`, this code has no special case for `.svg`; calling ImageMagick `convert` on an SVG to reduce file size can rasterize or otherwise alter the vector file, or fail. Large SVG uploads can therefore be corrupted or lose their original content.

No tests for automatic downsizing and changed upload limits

The PR introduces server-side image downsizing, changes URL download limits, and alters client-side upload validation, but no test files are added or updated. Without coverage for oversized images, failed conversions, SVG/GIF handling, and attachment limits, regressions in these upload paths are likely.

The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id]) can return nil if the user has no topic_users row for the topic (for example they have never visited it). GET /t/:topic_id/unsubscribe changes notification state

Because GET requests are exempt from Rails CSRF verification and the controller skips the XHR check, any page the user visits, or a browser/link prefetch, can issue a request to /t/<id>/unsubscribe with the user's session cookies and silently change their notification state. The controller updates the record with tu.save! rather than TopicUser.change. There are no controller/request specs for the new unsubscribe action. The PR changes state, adds redirects, and depends on TopicUser presence, but tests do not cover successful level changes, missing TopicUser, slug redirects, HTML vs JSON, or the unsafe GET behavior.

If the original `guests` array contains duplicates, blacklisted emails, existing attendee emails, or case variants, the wrong email template can be sent (for example, an existing attendee may be treated as a new guest). Pass the normalized `uniqueGuests` list that was actually inserted.

The candidate describes the same thing: the original guests list is passed instead of the filtered uniqueGuests, which causes the wrong email template to be sent. Both point to the same misclassification issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

Guest emails are not normalized or deduplicated server-side

In addGuestsHandler, `uniqueGuests` filters input emails case-sensitively and does not remove duplicates within the request. As a result, `guests: ["a@example.com", "A@Example.com"]` or repeated emails can create duplicate attendee rows or bypass the existing-attendee check. The blacklist comparison is also case-sensitive because only the blacklist is lowercased, so `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` can be bypassed with uppercase input. Normalize (trim/lowercase) and deduplicate guest emails before comparing, persisting, and sending emails.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate states explicitly that uniqueGuests does not remove duplicates within the request, so repeated emails can create duplicate attendee rows. This is the same issue as the golden comment. The candidate also raises a case-sensitivity point, which is extra but does not conflict with it.

`sendAddGuestsEmails` sends organizer/host and attendee emails unconditionally. Other email flows accept `eventTypeMetadata` and check `eventTypeDisableHostEmail`/`eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`, respecting `disableStandardEmails` settings. This new flow does not, so emails can be sent even when the event type is configured to suppress host or attendee standard emails. Pass and honor event-type metadata.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say sendAddGuestsEmails ignores the disableStandardEmails event-type metadata flags, so host and attendee emails can go out even when they are disabled. The candidate describes the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update uses requester's credentials instead of booking owner's credentials

addGuestsHandler constructs EventManager with `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`, even though the mutation is allowed for attendees and team admins/owners. External calendar events are normally owned by the booking organizer/host, so using the requester's credentials can fail to update the correct calendar or update nothing. The handler loads `booking.user.credentials` but does not use them. Use the booking owner/host (or the credentials associated with the destination calendar) for the calendar update.

No booking status check before adding guests

After loading the booking, addGuestsHandler only checks existence and permissions. It does not reject cancelled, rejected, or otherwise inactive bookings. The API can therefore add attendees to cancelled or past bookings, send notification emails, and attempt calendar updates for events that should no longer be modified. Add a status/eligibility check (for example, only upcoming accepted bookings unless intentionally broader).

Bookings without a user crash when looking up organizer

addGuestsHandler does `prisma.user.findFirstOrThrow({ where: { id: booking.userId || 0 } })`. For bookings where `userId` is null (possible for some team bookings), this queries user id 0 and throws, producing an error instead of handling the team/organizer case. The handler should support bookings without a direct user or fall back to the appropriate team/primary email.

Guests array is unbounded

The mutation schema allows `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no maximum length or minimum count. A client can submit an arbitrarily large number of emails, causing bulk attendee creation and mass email fan-out. Add a reasonable `.min(1).max(N)` and server-side uniqueness validation.

Error toast fallback is unreachable

In AddGuestsDialog, `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`;` always produces a non-empty string, so `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), ...)` never uses the fallback. If `err.data?.code` or `err.message` is missing, users may see `undefined: ...` instead of a friendly message. Build the message conditionally.

Dialog state is not consistently reset when closed

AddGuestsDialog resets `multiEmailValue` only on cancel or successful mutation, and does not reset `isInvalidEmail` on success. Closing via `onOpenChange` (for example, Escape or overlay click) leaves previous emails and validation errors in state, so reopening can show stale values or stale invalid-email warnings. Reset form state whenever the dialog closes or opens.

Hardcoded English tooltip in MultiEmail

The remove-email control uses `<Tooltip content="Remove email">`, which is not localized through `t()`. Users in non-English locales will see English text. Use a translation key.

No tests for new addGuests mutation

The PR introduces a privileged mutation with nontrivial permission checks, guest deduplication/case handling, blacklist filtering, calendar updates, and email selection, but no automated tests are included. Maintainers would want coverage for organizer/attendee/team admin permissions, cancelled bookings, duplicate/case-variant emails, blacklisted emails, and the email template selection.

If a user copies a code with surrounding whitespace or uppercase characters, a valid code will be rejected. The same normalization issue exists in the disable endpoint. Trim and lowercase user input before comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing reuse or resurrection of used codes

During login, the encrypted backup-code array is read, a matching index is set to null, and the user row is updated in a separate write. Concurrent successful logins can both read the same unused backup code before either update completes, allowing the same one-time code to be used more than once. Concurrent use of different codes can also cause last-write-wins to overwrite another request's nulling, effectively resurrecting a used code. This breaks the one-time-use guarantee. Use a transaction or an atomic/conditional update when consuming a backup code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: backup codes are read, mutated in memory, and written back non-atomically, so concurrent logins can reuse a single one-time backup code.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code blob URL is not revoked on close or unmount

The component creates an object URL containing the user's backup codes for download. It only revokes a previous URL when a new setup response is received. If the modal is closed, cancelled, or the component unmounts, the object URL remains alive for the page lifetime, unnecessarily retaining sensitive backup-code data in memory. Revoke the object URL during reset/cleanup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the backup-code object URL is never revoked when the component unmounts, so memory is retained. The candidate adds the sensitive-data angle and the modal-close case, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Password verification is skipped whenever a TOTP code is present, enabling second-factor-only login

In the credentials authorize function, the password is only verified when credentials.totpCode is absent. The new backup-code branch is selected whenever credentials.backupCode is present, even if credentials.totpCode is also present. As a result, a CAL user with a password can authenticate with only a valid TOTP code, and a valid backup code plus any non-empty totpCode also bypasses password verification. This defeats the first authentication factor for 2FA logins. Password verification should be required for accounts that have a password, especially for backup-code use, instead of being skipped whenever totpCode is present.

Backup-code login is blocked for non-CAL identity-provider accounts

The early checks for non-CAL identity providers only exempt credentials.totpCode, not credentials.backupCode. If a user with 2FA enabled has a non-CAL identity provider (for example after identity-provider conversion/linking), supplying a backup code without a TOTP code throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled or IncorrectEmailPassword. The disable endpoint supports backup codes, but the login flow effectively makes backup recovery unavailable for these accounts. The checks should also allow backupCode where appropriate.

Successful 2FA enable is not propagated if the modal is dismissed without clicking the explicit Close button

After the TOTP code is accepted, the modal moves to the backup-code screen and only calls onEnable when the user clicks the explicit Close button. If the dialog is dismissed through onOpenChange, such as ESC, backdrop click, or a parent-controlled close, onEnable is not called and the modal state is not reset. The settings screen can remain showing 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled on the server, and reopening the modal may show a stale step. The modal should handle close/dismiss by resetting state and notifying the parent appropriately.

E2E assertion checks a Promise instead of the actual checked state

The test uses await expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy(). locator.isChecked() returns a Promise, and asserting that the Promise is truthy does not verify that the switch is actually checked. This can pass even when 2FA was not enabled. The test also does not handle the new backup-code screen in this first flow. Use a web-first assertion such as toBeChecked() and handle the backup-code dialog.

No E2E coverage for backup-code login or one-time consumption

The PR adds backup-code login and consumes backup codes on use, but the E2E tests only verify that backup codes are displayed, copied, and downloaded during setup. There is no test that logs in with a backup code, verifies that a used backup code is rejected, or disables 2FA using a backup code. The TODO in the test file acknowledges this gap. These flows should be covered before merge.

Backup code can be submitted empty despite the input being marked required

The login form uses noValidate and the Zod schema only validates email/password while passing through other fields. When the user switches to the lost-access backup-code screen, the BackupCode input's required attribute is not enforced and there is no schema validation for backupCode. Submitting an empty backup code sends an empty value to the server, which then falls back to the TOTP path and returns a confusing second-factor-required error. Add validation for backupCode or avoid disabling native validation for this field.

Copy button shows success even if clipboard write fails

The copy handler calls navigator.clipboard.writeText without awaiting it or catching errors, then immediately shows a success toast. If the Clipboard API is unavailable, permission is denied, or the write rejects, the user still sees a success message, and an unhandled rejection may occur. Await the clipboard operation and show success only when it actually succeeds.

Disable-2FA modal state persists when closed via dialog controls

The modal does not reset twoFactorLostAccess, form values, or error message when the dialog is closed through onOpenChange rather than through Cancel or successful disable. If a user opens the lost-access view, closes the modal, and reopens it, the modal can unexpectedly remain in lost-access mode or retain stale input/error state. Reset modal state when the dialog is closed or reopened.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback credential filter uses impossible type 'calendar'

When destinationCalendar is missing or empty, the fallback selects this.calendarCredentials.filter(cred => cred.type === 'calendar'). The credentials collected here are types such as google_calendar or office365_calendar and are filtered by endsWith('_calendar'), so an exact 'calendar' type will not exist. The fallback therefore never creates a traditional calendar event.

Team destination calendars are dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null when neither eventType nor organizer has a calendar. The later collective-only code uses evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars), which is a no-op on null. All team host calendars are discarded, so collective hosts will not receive calendar events.

loadUsers can return undefined instead of an empty array

The new loadUsers returns users.length ? users : eventType.users, while the old code returned eventType.users || []. If hosts is empty and eventType.users is undefined, loadUsers resolves to undefined; downstream code that expects an array, such as users.length or users[0], can throw.

Google event patch can use undefined calendarId

selectedCalendar can be undefined when no destination calendar matches the credential. The insert call falls back to 'primary', but the follow-up patch call passes calendarId: selectedCalendar without the same fallback. This can fail to update the event description with the hangout link or produce an unhandled API error.

Google createEvent selects calendar only by credentialId

CalendarManager passes the destination calendar externalId, but Google createEvent chooses the calendar only by matching credentialId. If the same credential has multiple possible destination calendars, the first match is used instead of the intended externalId, so the event can be created in the wrong calendar and the stored externalId can be wrong.

Lark createEvent always uses first destination calendar

For collective events, EventManager creates an event for each host credential, but Lark createEvent always uses event.destinationCalendar[0].externalId. When a non-main host credential is used, it will attempt to create the event in the first host's calendar or fail, so multiple-host Lark calendars are not handled correctly.

Office 365 createEvent always uses first destination calendar

Office 365 createEvent always uses the first entry of event.destinationCalendar to build /me/calendars/{externalId}/events. For collective multiple hosts, secondary host credentials will target the first host's calendar or fall back incorrectly, so events may be created in the wrong calendar or fail.

updateLocation creates references without credential or external calendar IDs

referencesToCreate maps result.externalId and result.credentialId, but CalendarManager.updateEvent does not populate these fields. editLocation.handler then creates booking references with null credentialId/externalCalendarId, which can break later updates, reschedules, or cancellations that rely on those references.

Reschedule merge deletes only first old calendar reference

When merging/rescheduling with newBookingId, only the first old calendar reference is found and deleted. For collective bookings with multiple host calendar references, the other old calendar events are left behind.

Video credentialId is dropped in create references

In create(), credentialId is only preserved for calendar results; non-calendar results such as video now get credentialId: undefined. If createMeeting returns a credentialId, it is dropped from referencesToCreate, making later video updates rely on ambiguous type matching.

Duplicate events for non-traditional calendars

createAllCalendarEvents processes destinationCalendar entries and then unconditionally creates events for every credential whose type includes 'other_calendar'. If a destinationCalendar entry is itself an other_calendar integration, this creates duplicate events.

createEvent reports success when calendar adapter is unavailable

createEvent initializes success to true and does not set it false when getCalendar returns null. It then returns a successful EventResult with no createdEvent, which can cause callers to store or reference a calendar event that was never created.

Awaiting array instead of promises

In the paid cancellation branch, await apiDeletes awaits the array itself rather than the promises it contains. The handler can return before calendar/video deletions finish, and rejected delete promises may become unhandled.

Recurring cancellation deletes wrong or duplicate calendar events

For recurring cancellations, inside each calendar reference the code iterates all user calendar credentials and deletes the first calendar reference found on each updated booking. This can use the wrong credential, delete the same event multiple times, and miss events belonging to other calendar references or hosts.

Confirming a collective booking only includes one destination calendar

When confirming a booking, evt.destinationCalendar is built only from booking.destinationCalendar or the confirming user's destination calendar. For collective events, other hosts' destination calendars are not included, so EventManager.create will not create calendar events for all hosts.

Stripe payment success only includes one destination calendar

handlePaymentSuccess builds evt.destinationCalendar from a single booking/user calendar. For paid collective events, other hosts' destination calendars are omitted, so their calendar events will not be created after payment confirmation.

PayPal payment success only includes one destination calendar

handlePaymentSuccess builds evt.destinationCalendar from a single booking/user calendar. For paid collective events, other hosts' destination calendars are omitted, so their calendar events will not be created after PayPal payment confirmation.

Webhook/API payload contract changed for destinationCalendar

CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar changed from a singular object/null to an array. Webhook payloads and other external consumers that expect the previous shape may break, for example null vs [] vs object. If intentional, this contract change should be documented; otherwise external payloads should preserve the old shape.
